title: Straight-line graphs you will actually use
hook: A motor winding's resistance, read at a few temperatures, plots roughly as a line. How do you turn those readings into a rule for other temperatures in that range, and what do its two numbers mean?
oneBreath: Any straight line on a graph that is not vertical has a rule, y = mx + c, with just two numbers in it. The gradient m is how much y changes for each 1 along, found from any two points on the line, and c is the value of y where the line crosses the y-axis. Two points, or one point and a gradient, pin down one line and its rule, and the same two points also give their distance apart and their midpoint. On the job, readings that fall on or near a line become a law, where the gradient and the crossing are real quantities with units, such as a resistor's ohms.

ideas.title: Gradient from two points
ideas.oneLine: A line's gradient m is change in y ÷ change in x between any two of its points: the rise for each 1 along.

ideas.title: Distance and midpoint
ideas.oneLine: The step triangle between two points also gives their distance apart, by Pythagoras, and their midpoint, halfway along and halfway up.

ideas.title: y = mx + c
ideas.oneLine: Any line that is not vertical has a rule y = mx + c, with m its gradient and c where it crosses the y-axis.

ideas.title: Finding the equation of a line
ideas.oneLine: From two points, or a point and the gradient, get m, then put one point into y = mx + c and solve for c.

ideas.title: Laws from readings
ideas.oneLine: When readings plot as a straight line, its gradient and y-axis crossing are real quantities with units, like a resistor's ohms from volts against amps.

ideas.title: Fitting a line to readings
ideas.oneLine: When real readings scatter, lay one line through their middle, about as many above as below, and read the law from that line.

calibration.q: A line passes through the points (2, 3) and (2, 8). How steep is it, as a rise for each 1 along?
options: It has no such number: it stands straight up
calibration.why: Both points have x = 2, so the line stands straight up. Its run is 0, and rise ÷ run would mean 5 ÷ 0, which has no answer. 0 is the steepness of a flat line, where the rise is 0, not the run.

calibration.q: The line y = 2x − 6 is drawn on a grid. Where does it cross the x-axis, the one running across?
calibration.why: Everywhere on the x-axis y is 0, so 0 = 2x − 6, which gives x = 3: the point (3, 0). (0, −6) is where the line crosses the other axis, the y-axis running up the side.
